scope: Only reads archived cheaper/equal flags, identities and existing summaries; no loss/cost recalculation, model fitting, selection, new data, or experiment.

reference_and_slice_bindings.archived_value: Exact floating equality; cheaper iff difference<0. No threshold/tolerance chosen from outcomes.
mF=mean(C_F-B), computed separately on each full comparison grid in source units; beta=b/mF, so actual fixed-breach amount is beta*mF. kappa and c are per-unit amounts.

Per-issued-report cost, not sum over overlapping holding periods, optimized policy, observed coefficients or common-dollar cross-market portfolio. The illustrative/not-observed-real-cost sentence appears once in Limitations.

denominator.derivation: Unique normalized_source x window in the matched row bindings; 17 contracts x 2 windows = 34, no pooled independence claim.

sorted_grid.center_rule: Middle sorted position on each odd-length archived axis; no interpolation or arithmetic midpoint.

direction: Expanded QR33 is more often cheaper than F toward higher reserve coefficients and lower fixed-breach charges, with one contract/history exception to monotonicity.

MCS.wording: Nearly always describes 90/98=91.8% of these related comparisons, not unique superiority or predictive-risk equality; prefer exact wording 'in 90 of 98 comparisons'.

menu_and_M2.wording: The constant-arm short-history median excess loss falls from 116.24327967680179% to 0.2069371499562489% (116.2% to 0.2% at one decimal); switching is 121.40097999787356% to -0.22777914491914353%. M2=-0.43471629487539243 percentage points misses the registered +5-point threshold. This does not establish no effect or equivalence.

recommended_cost_subsection_exactly_thre: At fixed $c=1$, expanded-menu QR33 is generally cheaper than F more often with higher reserve coefficient $\kappa$ and lower fixed-breach coefficient $\beta$, although the archived grid is not monotone.

Across the 17 contracts and two histories, it is strictly cheaper in 5/34 comparisons at the sorted-grid centre $(\kappa,\beta)=(0.1,0.25)$, versus 32/34 at $(1,0)$ and 1/34 at the opposite corner $(0.01,5)$.
These coefficients are illustrative preferences rather than observed business costs, so the rankings do not establish funding gains or a cost-optimal policy.
recommended_contribution_3: Third, score gains translate into lower limit costs only in parts of the coefficient grid; CFTC expanded-regression cost advantages are more prevalent under higher reserve and lower fixed-breach charges, with exceptions to monotonicity.
recommended_RQ3_answer: For RQ3, score gains imply lower limit costs only for some illustrative reserve, breach-frequency and exceedance preferences; the CFTC grid generally favors expanded regression as reserve charges rise and fixed-breach charges fall, with exceptions to monotonicity.
recommended_letter: The third finding separates forecast-score gains from limit-cost rankings: expanded regression is generally cheaper in more CFTC comparisons under higher reserve and lower fixed-breach charges, while the illustrative coefficient grid contains exceptions to monotonicity.
